To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) AKT can protect cancer cells from drug-induced apoptosis independent of its catalytic kinase activity; (2) AKT protects cancer cells through its PH domain; and (3) the PH domain of AKT is a potential target for cancer therapy.

1) a kinase-independent function is required for the survival of cancer cells harboring oncogenic mutations in MET, HER-2 or PI3K; 2) this function is mediated by AKT's PH-domain; 3) this function can be blocked by allosteric inhibitors of AKT, but not ATP-competitive inhibitors.
a kinase independent function of AKT protects cancer cells from drug-induced cell death.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of the molecular mechanisms that regulate the function of the serine/threonine kinase AKTs.
the development of new therapeutic agents for the treatment of cancer.
the identification and characterization of novel functions of the serine/threonine kinase AKTi, a kinase that is frequently activated in cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
AKT has two different functions: a kinase-dependent function and a kinase-independent function.
“AKT has a kinase independent function that promotes cancer cell survival”.
AKT is not only an important kinase, but also an important scaffold protein, and this is the first report of a non-enzymatic function of AKT in cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
AKT can promote cell survival independent of its kinase function, which has important implications for the use of AKT inhibitors in cancer therapy.
the kinase activity of AKT is not required for its ability to promote cell survival, but instead it is a conformational change in AKT that is important for its survival promoting functions.
the AKT kinase domain is not required for the pro-survival activity of AKT.
The main takeaway from our work is that
AKT has a kinase-independent function that can be exploited to promote cancer cell survival.
the PH domain is an important regulator of AKT function.
the kinase-independent function is a general feature of AKT, which is conserved from yeast to humans and is independent of the kinase domain.
